title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Anna, in that first period of her emancipation and her quick return to health, felt unforgivably happy and full of the joy of life. The thought of her husband's unhappiness did not poison her happiness. On one side that memory was too dreadful to be looked at. On the other side, her husband's unhappiness had given her too much happiness to be regretted. The memory of everything that had happened after her illness — her reconciliation with her husband, its breakdown, the news of Vronsky's wound, his visit, the preparations for divorce, the leaving of her husband's house, the parting from her son — all of it seemed to her like a feverish dream from which she had woken up alone with Vronsky abroad. The thought of the harm done to her husband stirred a feeling in her like revulsion, something like what a drowning man might feel after shaking off another man who was clinging to him. That man did drown. It was a wicked act, of course, but it was the only way out, and better not to brood over such terrible facts.

One consoling reflection on her behavior had come to her at the very moment of the final break, and now, recalling all the past, she remembered that one thought. "I have unavoidably made that man miserable," she thought, "but I don't want to profit by his misery. I too am suffering, and shall suffer; I'm losing what I valued above everything — I'm losing my good name and my son. I've done wrong, and so I don't want happiness, I don't want a divorce, and shall suffer from my disgrace and from being separated from my child." But however sincerely Anna had meant to suffer, she was not suffering. There was no shame. With the tact both of them had in such large supply, they had managed to avoid Russian ladies abroad, and so had never put themselves in a false position, and everywhere they had met people who pretended to understand their situation perfectly — far better, in fact, than they did themselves. Separation from the son she loved — even that did not cause her real anguish in these early days. The baby girl — _his_ child — was so sweet, and had so won Anna's heart, being all that was left to her, that Anna rarely thought of her son.

The desire for life, growing stronger with her recovered health, was so intense, and the circumstances of life were so new and pleasant, that Anna felt unforgivably happy. The more she got to know Vronsky, the more she loved him. She loved him both for himself and for his love of her. To have him completely her own was a continuous joy. His presence was always sweet to her. Every trait of his character, which she came to know better and better, was unspeakably dear to her. His appearance, changed by civilian dress, was as attractive to her as if she were a young girl in love. In everything he said, thought, and did, she saw something especially noble and elevated. Her adoration of him alarmed her, in fact; she searched in him for anything that wasn't fine, and could not find it. She did not dare let him see her sense of how insignificant she was beside him. She felt that, if he knew, he might stop loving her sooner; and she dreaded nothing now so much as losing his love, even though she had no reason to fear it. But she could not help being grateful to him for the way he treated her, and showing that she appreciated it. He, who in her view had such a clear gift for a political career — one in which he would certainly have played a leading part — had sacrificed his ambition for her sake, and never showed the slightest sign of regret. He was more lovingly respectful to her than ever, and his constant care that she should never feel the awkwardness of her position never left him for a single instant. He, so manly a man, never opposed her — indeed had no will of his own with her, and was anxious, it seemed, for nothing but to anticipate her wishes. And she could not help appreciating this, even though the very intensity of his concern for her, the atmosphere of care he surrounded her with, sometimes weighed on her.

Vronsky, meanwhile, in spite of the complete realization of what he had so long wanted, was not perfectly happy. He soon felt that the realization of his desires had given him no more than a grain of sand out of the mountain of happiness he had been expecting. It showed him the mistake men make in picturing happiness as the realization of their desires. For a time after joining his life to hers and putting on civilian dress, he had felt all the delight of freedom in general, which he had known nothing of before, and of freedom in his love — and he was content, but not for long. He soon realized that there was springing up in his heart a desire for desires — _ennui_. Without meaning to, he began grasping at every passing whim, mistaking it for a desire and an object. Sixteen hours of the day had to be filled somehow, since they were living abroad in complete freedom, outside the framework of social life that filled up the time in Petersburg. As for the amusements of bachelor existence, which had kept Vronsky entertained on previous trips abroad, those were out of the question, since the one attempt of the kind had led to a sudden bout of depression in Anna, quite out of proportion to its cause — a late supper with bachelor friends. Relations with the local society — foreign and Russian — were equally out of the question, given the irregularity of their position. Sightseeing — apart from the fact that everything had already been seen — did not, for Vronsky, a Russian and a sensible man, carry the enormous significance Englishmen are able to attach to it.
And just as a hungry stomach eagerly seizes on anything it can get, hoping to find nourishment in it, Vronsky, quite unconsciously, grabbed first at politics, then at new books, then at pictures.

Since he had had a taste for painting from childhood, and since, not knowing what else to spend his money on, he had started collecting engravings, he came to a stop at painting, began to take an interest in it, and concentrated on it the unoccupied mass of desires that were demanding satisfaction.

He had a quick eye for art, and probably, with his taste for imitating art, he supposed himself to have the real thing that's essential for an artist — and after some hesitation over which style of painting to pick — religious, historical, realistic, or genre painting — he set to work to paint. He could appreciate all kinds and could have felt inspired by any of them; but he had no conception of the possibility of knowing nothing at all about any school of painting, and of being inspired directly by what is inside one's soul, without minding whether what one paints belongs to any recognized school. Since he knew nothing of this, and drew his inspiration not directly from life but indirectly from life as embodied in art, his inspiration came very quickly and easily, and just as quickly and easily came his success in painting something very similar to the kind of painting he was trying to imitate.

More than any other style, he liked the French — graceful and effective — and in that style he began painting Anna's portrait in Italian costume, and the portrait seemed to him, and to everyone who saw it, extremely successful.
